source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Did you know that a 14th-century Muslim scholar described supply and demand, the division of labor, and the labor theory of value, four hundred years before Adam Smith? In this pilot episode, we trace the entire arc of Islamic economic thought: from the bustling markets of pre-Islamic Mecca and the Prophet Muhammad's career as a merchant, through the golden age of scholars like Abu Yusuf, Al-Ghazali, and Ibn Khaldun, to the colonial disruption and the remarkable modern revival of Islamic finance. Topics: Pre-Islamic Trade, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), Riba & Zakat, Golden Age Scholars, Ibn Khaldun, Trade Networks, Modern Revival Series: Historical Islamic Economics (Part I) • Episode 1 of 6

thread: Ibn Khaldun described supply and demand, the division of labor, and the labor theory of value in the 14th century. Four hundred years before Adam Smith.
The Prophet Muhammad was a merchant before his calling. Islamic economics didn't emerge from theory—it grew from the marketplaces of Mecca.
Abu Yusuf and Al-Ghazali developed sophisticated frameworks for trade, prohibition of riba, and wealth distribution during Islam's golden age.
Modern Islamic finance is a revival, not an invention. The principles were tested in trading networks that spanned from Spain to Southeast Asia. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-1

linkedin.post: The story of Islamic economics begins not in modern boardrooms, but in the bustling markets of 7th-century Mecca. Before his prophetic mission, Muhammad (PBUH) was a successful merchant. This wasn't incidental—it shaped how early Islamic civilization approached trade, wealth, and economic justice. By the 14th century, Ibn Khaldun had articulated supply and demand, the division of labor, and labor theory of value. Four centuries before Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations. Scholars like Abu Yusuf and Al-Ghazali developed sophisticated frameworks around riba prohibition, zakat distribution, and market regulation. These weren't abstract theories—they governed trade networks spanning from Al-Andalus to Southeast Asia. Today's Islamic finance revival draws from this deep well of economic thought, adapting centuries-old principles to modern markets. Listen to the full story: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-1
